regularities, defaults, or improper conduct on the part of any one in connection with an election. If hon. members would do that it would save us a lot of time spent in debating matters here. I know that if we went into the past electoral history of my hon. friend's constituency we could be very acrimonious, but we should not get very far. There are many people in that constituency that neither of us would trust in connection with an election. But if an officer has, in the opinion of my hon. friend, misunderstood or failed to do his duty, there is the place to make the report; and if legislative intervention is necessary, the Chief Electoral Officer, before Parliament meets, can not only make his report but'draft adequate legislation to protect the interests of the people. We should get very much further ahead by such a method, and I would suggest that that be done. I might say that in regard to the very matter I spoke of a few moments ago, as well as touching several other matters that came under my observation, I made a report to the electoral officer. Fortunately, in my constituency I did not have a single complaint to make in regard to any one, and I was very glad of the fact. I trust that when the time comes the Government will keep the electoral officer working and let him submit a bill, the Government acting merely as sponsor, so that the legislation might be as non-partisan and as useful as possible.

The hon. senior member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter), said that I should have made a report to the Chief Electoral Officer, as he did. Well, I do not see any amendments in acordance with the recommendations he made to him. The amendment which is before the committee I moved for the purpose of bringing it to the attention of the Government in order that it might receive their consideration, and perhaps might impress upon them the necessity for a great number of changes in the Election Act. However, I am perfectly willing to withdraw the amendment in view of the statement made by the Prime Minister that an opportunity will be given to amend that act.
Bill, as amended, reported, read the third time, and passed.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 70, to amend The Fisheries Act, 1914.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1.-Penalty for leaving any port in Canada with intent to fish for salmon or lobsters in sea beyond territorial waters.
What changes are contemplated?

There are no changes; the section is merely to confirm by statute regulations that already exist. Both lobster and salmon fishing are carried on not only inside territorial waters, but outside as well, and if there were no regulations with regard to fishing outside, the fisheries would undoubtedly be depleted within a short time. There is nothing new in the principle; it has always been understood, and up to the present time there has been no attempt to violate the intention of the regulation. It has come to the notice of the department, however, that in some sections of the country people who are not given licenses are prepared to challenge the authority of the Government restraining them from fishing outside territorial waters. As a matter of fact the lobster fisheries regulations have always contained a provision of this kind, as do the British Columbia salmon regulations. It is the opinion of the Department of Justice that it is better for us to have this regulation enacted in legislation instead of merely being enforced as at present. I may add that the United States have a similar provision in their fisheries law.
All that is being done, therefore, is to enact in the form of a statute regulations that are already in force.
Exactly.

Section agreed to.
On section 2.-Burden of proof.

Does the minister not think that perhaps, in view of the fact that the magistracy of the country is not always of the calibre that one would like to see, it is going a little too far to place the burden of proof in this matter on the accused? If such an accused were tried before a jury he would have more chances of getting off, even if the burden of proof were put upon him, than he would have before a magistrate when that burden rests upon him. The magistrates, somehow, especially the less business they have, seem
281S
Fisheries Act Amdt.

to think that it is their duty to convict a man who is brought before them; the assumption seems to be that he must be guilty if he comes before them. The burden of proving absence of intent or knowledge lies with the person accused, and I should be sorry indeed to be called upon to prove that on behalf of the most worthy client I ever had, before a certain species of magistrate with whom I have come in contact. The section goes rather too far; it should be enough if there is at least a prima facie case made against the accused. But to have imposed upon one the absolute burden of proving innocence is further than our laws go, except with regard to whiskey.

I appreciate what the minister is endeavouring to get at. The regulations apply practically only to our own Canadian people, and they cover fishing in extra-territorial waters as well as in the territorial area. I presume these regulations are intended to apply particularly to lobster fishing. There is a section of the Fisheries Act that provides that no person shall offer for sale, or have in his posession, lobsters caught in a manner or at a time prohibited by law. Prior to amendment the act contained a clause to the effect that:
No one shall without lawful excuse, the proof whereof shall lie on him, have in his possession fish caught at a time or in a manner prohibited by law.
It was found very difficult to prove that the fish were caught "at a time or in a manner prohibited by law." Now that the act is being amended, the minister undoubtedly wants the amendment to apply to extraterritorial waters. But I quite agree with my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Baxter) that it is almost an outrage to place this burden of proof in all cases upon the defendant. In my short experience as a legal practitioner in Nova Scotia, I regret to say, usually I have found the magistrates are not fit persons to administer justice. As the hon. member for St. John says, the mere fact that a person is brought before the court is usually regarded as conclusive evidence that he should be convicted. If cases were dealt with by a court of competent jurisdiction, you would feel that justice would be administered; but to cast the burden of proof upon the accused who is at the mercy of the magistrate is, I think, going too far. In fact, the whole tenor of criminal and quasi-criminal legislation seems to be to

cast on the accused the burden of proving himself innocent rather than that the prosecution should prove him guilty. I do not believe this sub-section is necessary at all, and I would urge the minister to strike it from the bill, because there is ample provision to deal with these cases under our present law. Do not compel a man to prove himself innocent who is charged by some officious officer or half detective on very slight evidence perhaps of some such offence as this subsection is intended to cover. I move that section 2 of the bill be struck out.

This affects British
Columbia as well as the other maritime provinces, and if this clause is struck out I know that the effect of the bill will be vitiated entirely in British Columbia. It is extremely difficult in cases of this kind to prove intent, especially among certain. classes of foreigners. Therefore I submit that, with all due regard to our legal tradition, which place the onus of proof upon the prosecution, there are some circumstances, as in the present case, where that tradition may safely be departed from. In this case the fine is not very burdensome, and the purpose is to aid an important industry. The bill as drafted is intended to meet special circumstances, all of which are not before the House. I think the clause should be accepted.

I cannot help but
think that it is setting a dangerous precedent to say that a man accused of crime must prove himself innocent. It is contrary to British justice, and I know the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) is pretty good at quoting British precedents. One can imagine a case, an extreme one it may be, where a fishery inspector having a grudge against a certain man could put him to all sorts of expense and annoyance by accusing him of intent to break the law as set forth in this section. I do not think you should prosecute a man before he puts his intentions into execution. Therefore, I think that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) is sound.
I do not think we should pass special legislation to meet the very lawless condition in British Columbia referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) , and so put in jeopardy the law-abiding citizens of the eastern maritime provinces.

I would suggest to the minister that he report progress on this

Canada Shipping Act
bill and have the clause redrafted along the lines of making the possession of certain things or the doing of certain acts prima facie evidence of guilt, rather than require the accused to absolutely prove his innocence. No doubt the officers in this department will advise my hon. friend as to what could be fairly taken as prima facie evidence of intent. The difficulty is that the penalty does not stop even at $1,000, but that the whole catch, the vessel itself, the gear and everything may be forfeited. That may be done by one justice of the peace, and he may be very much prejudiced against the accused. At first I was inclined to agree with the suggestion of my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Martell), but on further consideration I think that if adopted it might be going a little too far in the other direction. I can see the difficulties in the minds of other members. There should be what I might term a half-way house, by which, while the accused would not be able to escape the law too easily, yet at the same time he would not be absolutely ruined through perhaps not even a feeling of spite, hut an ignorant desire on the part of some official to do what he thinks is right.

I agree that on general principles it is dangerous to put the burden of proof of his innocence on the accused party; but, as my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) said, this is a special law intended to meet special conditions, and if this provision, or one of a similar nature, is not inserted in the bill perhaps the purpose of this legislation would not be achieved. I do not see that the section as drafted would work any great hardship, because after all a person cannot go fishing without a license, and the moment a man is caught fishing without a license, the purport of the law is accomplished and it should be for him to prove that he does not come within its provisions. However, I am willing to accept the suggestion of my jion. friend from St. John (Mr. Baxter) and will ask that the committee rise and report progress so that the clause can be redrafted to meet the objections raised.
There is nothing wrong with the clause. Let us go ahead and put it through.

There is something
wrong with it.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. Ernest Lapointe (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) Bill No. 79, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Pilotage) was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon Mr. Gordon in the Chair.	*
On section 1-Foreign ships of war and hospital ships may be made exempt ships.

Under the Pilotage
Act all ships have to pay pilotage dues whether or not they require the services of a pilot. There are some exceptions, and this bill is for the purpose of adding to those exceptions., The first amendment exempts from the payment of pilotage dues the ships of war and hospi-5.p.m. tal ships belonging to such fore-eign nations as may be specified by the. Governor in Council. The idea is to extend that privilege to those nations which grant a similar privilege to British warships. As a matter of fact, in practice they never have been required to pay the dues; the amendment is to bring the law into accord with recognized practice. The second exception excludes ships registered in Canada which are engaged exclusively in fishing. These ships have not been compelled to pay the pilotage dues in the past. The amendment is to prevent any difficulties which might arise from the fact that under the law as it now stands these vessels could be compelled to pay such dues.

I am quite in accord with
these amendments, especially the first, which says that ships of war and hospital ships belonging to such foreign nation or nations as may be specified by the Governor in Council shall be exempt from the payment of pilotage dues. If only as a matter of courtesy, Canada should be quite willing to pilot ships of war of other nations, so long as they are friendly nations, into our ports without asking them to pay pilotage dues. Everybody will agree that so far as hospital ships are concerned .the amendment is a good one. Subsection (j) however, provides that the following ships shall also be exempt:
*Ships registered in Canada engaged exclusively in fishing.
I suggest that the word "exclusively" be struck out. A great many fishing vessels, after they put dn the season's fishing from, say, January until October, go coasting or

Canada Shipping Act

freighting, and you are going to have a mix-up if you leave the word "exclusively" in.	*
Why not make it read, " while engaged exclusively in fishing "?

No; that would not serve my purpose. These fishing vessels are small schooners; they are not really coasting or freighting vessels. They are not engaged all the time in coasting or freighting, but if they can enter a harbour while engaged in the fishing business without paying these dues, they should be able to do so while engaged in coasting or freighting in the fall.
Is it not a fact that these vessels never employ a pilot?
They do not; the captains of these vessels are as good men as the pilots themselves.

Under the present
act they could be compelled to pay pilotage dues, although they never avail themselves of the pilotage?
Exactly.
Are they ever charged pilotage?
Oh, yes.
Those engaged in fishing are not.
Yes, those over a certain number of tons, I think.
I do not object to the striking out of the word " exclusively
Amendment agreed to.

I move that the following subclause be added to clause 1 of the bill:
2.	Subparagraph (1) of paragraph (c) of the said subsection one is repealed, and the following is substituted in lieu thereof:
"(i) employed in trading from port to port in the same province, or employed in any one port or harbour, or
As the law is to-day the exception reads as follows:
(i) employed in trading from port to port in the same province.
A case arose the other day of a ship which was engaged in trading, not from one port to another port in the province, but from one part of a port to another part of the same port. As the law stands, that ship was not exempt and the amendment is to cover cases of that kind.
Amendment agreed to.

Where you
have coastal business going on between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia why should you discriminate at all?
There is a special provision for that.
Are you going to look after that?

There is a provision already in the bill dealing with trading between any or all of the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. I move, also, Mr. Chairman, that the following be added to clause 1 of the bill as subsection "k".
Vessels engaged in salvage or towing operations.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

On motion of Hon. G. P. Graham (Minister of Militia and Defence) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend The Air Board Act, chapter 11 of the statutes of 1919 (1st Session), to provide that the Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing the compensation to be paid, the persons to whom, and the manner in which, such compensation shall be payable, for the death or injury resulting directly from a flight undertaken in the course of duty in the public service of Canada of any person employed in the public service of Canada, or employed under the direction of any department of the public service of Canada: Provided, however, that such regulations shall mot extend to the payment of compensation for any death, or injury in respect of which provision for the payment of compensation, or a gratuity or pension is made by any other act.

Explain.
Mr. GRAHAM. In chapter 11 of the statutes of 1919, will be found the following section:
It shall be the duty of the Air Board,-
(l)	to consider, draft, and prepare for approval by the Governor in Council such regulations as may be considered necessary for the control or operation of aeronautics in Canada or within the limit of the territorial waters of Canada, and,
(m)	to perform such other duties as the Governor in Council may from time to time impose.
Section 5 provides that:
The Air Board shall have power to employ such officers and men under this act-

Air Board Act Amdt.
That is the Air Board Act-
-as may be authorized by the Governor in Council, under such conditions as to discipline and pay as the Governor in Council may determine,-
And so on. Under the provisions of that act an Order in Council was passed on May 29, 1920, setting out what should be paid to the dependents of an aviator in case he was killed, also the amounts that would be paid in case he was injured. Now the question has arisen whether the statute really gave such full authority, and this is to make it clear that that authority does exist. That is to say, the authority may exist but it has been questioned. The existing legislation would only apply to the civil aviator, but, in carrying on the operations of the air force, employees of the Forestry branch of the Interior Department sometimes accompany the aviators in order to make explorations and observatons of forest lands. Under the old Order in Council such persons would not be covered by any provision for a gratuity in case of injury. The legislation to be founded on this resolution will enable the Governor in Council to make regulations that will include any employee of the government.
In other words what you did in the past was merely to look after the pilot and not his passenger?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not the other civil employee.
Who was also engaged upon your work?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
It seems to be proper expenditure. What do you seek to prevent by your proviso? Give the committee a concrete case.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Let us say that the Forestry branch of the Department of the Interior wishes to send a man up with the aviator. That man, who is employed by another department, and is not in the civil . aviation force, would not, under the Order in Council, be eligible for a gratuity.

You have already explained that point. What I want to know is why the resolution contains the proviso which says:
Provided, however, that such regulations shall not extend to the payment of compensation for any death, or injury in respect of which provision for the payment of compensation, or a gratuity or pension is made by any other act.
What is the precise matter in view there?
179i

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A man who is entitled
to a gratuity under the Military Pensions' Act cannot draw two gratuities, or his dependents cannot draw both the gratuity under this act, and under the Military Pensions' Act as well.

Is there any
reason why, if this is the greater, he should not get it? If you provide, as a matter of fairness, a greater gratuity-as you very likely will-for accidents occuring from aeronautics, should not the party have the right to get whichever was the greater?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It might work out that way. It is possible that, on entering the Air Service, he might give up his right to the gratuity under the Military Pensions' Act.
I suggest that whichever is the greater should be given.

Does this bill cover
the case where a man might be part of the time engaged in military service and part of the time in some other department of the service? I have in mind a case which came before our committee regarding a man named Holland.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I might say that the
wife of Major Holland was paid $7,500 under the Order in Council, and she also gets paid, not under the Military Pensions' Act or anything of that kind but under the Soldiers' Insurance Act she also gets, I think, $5,000.

I am drafting a proposed amendment to read something like this:
Unless the compensation otherwise payable hereunder be in excess of such gratuity or pension payable under such other act, and in such case only to the extent of such excess.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no objection to the principle. My hon. friend might move that amendment to the bill.
Resolution reported, read the second time and cohcurred in. Mr. Graham, thereupon, moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 136 to amend the Air Board Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. Ernest Lapointe (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) Bill 106, to amend the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners Act, was read the second
Vancouver Harbour Bill

time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1-Section amended so as to repeal power to appoint port warden and deputy.
What is the change?

Under the Harbour Commissioners' Act, 1913, the corporation of the harbour commissioners may appoint a harbour master, deputy harbour master, port warden, deputy port warden, shipping master and deputy shipping masters. This bill is to strike out the words "port warden, deputy port warden, shipping master and deputy shipping master." Under the Shipping Act, those officers are under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Such a provision does not exist with regard to the port warden and shipping masters in the other harbours, for the very reason that it is the duty of those officers to see that the provisions of the act and the regulations of the department are complied with. None of their powers or duties has any relation to or connection with the powers of the harbour commissioners. They are officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and it is an anomaly that, in the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners Act, the harbour commissioners should have the right to control, to appoint, or to supervise the acts or duties of those officers. It is to make the act apply to Vancouver as it applies to the other harbours of the country.
Can the hon. minister tells us how the matter comes up? Has any inefficient work been done at Vancouver recently? Have any men been got rid of?

No, nothing of the
kind. This is suggested by officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, in order that the law may be uniform anywhere.

When was
this difficulty discovered? there is usually some reason for a provision of this kind?
I do not know. I was not the discoverer of that anomaly.
Perhaps you can find out from the deputy?

I am informed that this difficulty has been noticed many times during the last few years, but especially 
last year the shipping master got into difficulties with the British Board of Trade with regard to certain funds and the Board of Trade at Vancouver, of course, reported and applied to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which, under the law as it is, had no control over that officer, although he is the officer who applies the laws and regulations of the department.
There must be some reason why the act was framed in the way in which it now exists.
So far as is known in the department, there never was any reason for it. I may assure my hon. friend that there is no ultimate or secret reason.
No "joker".
No "joker". This is merely and simply to make the law as it should be.
I understand, from what the minister says, that he is following precisely what is done at Montreal, Quebec, Toronto and everywhere else.
Yes.
I should like the list to be clearly defined, of appointments to be made by the Government under this. What are they?
The shipping master and the port warden are the only ones.
The only two?
Yes.
Is there a vacancy in the positions of shipping master and port warden at the moment?
No.
Will there be?
I cannot speak for the future. Not that I know of presently.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. D. D. McKenzie (Solicitor General) Bill No. 123, to amend the Admiralty Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Governor in Council may appoint a deputy registrar for any district or registry division.

What is the object of this?

Admiralty ist Amdt.

As regards clause 1, under the old act, the Governor in Council appointed a registrar and the deputy registrar was appointed by the registrar. It was thought best that the governor in Council, who had authority to appoint a registrar, should also have power to appoint a deputy registrar. To make the change it is necessary only to insert the words "a deputy registrar." '
Why is it that the man who ought to know best should not appoint the deputy registrar?

In our own case, in the province of Nova Scotia, we have an admiralty division in the city of Halifax, where the registrar is appointed. We have also an admiralty division at Sydney in the island of Cape Breton. The registrar who resides at Halifax, some three hundred miles away, does not know the kind of man that should be deputy registrar in the city of Sydney nearly as well as the Bar Association, for instance, in that city. I think the Governor in Council who appoints the registrar should also have power to appoint the deputy registrar who, to all intents and purposes, is a separate officer, over whom the registrar has no control at all.
Is there a deputy registrar there now? How has the business been carried on in the past?

The business has been carried on in the past by a deputy who was appointed by Order in Council some years ago; but that Order in Council gave him jurisdiction over only four counties instead of sixteen counties. At Halifax, the registrar has full sway over the province; but while we have a court in the Cape Breton end of the province, we have a deputy registrar having jurisdiction over only four counties, and it would appear that the registrar at Halifax is not willing to give him any more jurisdiction as it might possibly be interfering with his territory. We think that our authorities ought to have power to deal with ships arriving in iSydney harbour, from whatever quarter they may come, and in regard to which proceedings in Admiralty are necessary, and not be confined entirely to something that might arise in the four counties of Cape Breton. We want the power to be vested in the Governor in Council to give us a deputy who will have jurisdiction all over the province.

If I understand my hon. friend aright, this is not
necessary for the purpose of a new appointment. It is not proposed to get rid of the present registrar in Cape Breton.
I have no intention of getting rid of him; I intend to reappoint him.
The intention seems to be to enlarge his jurisdiction at the expense of the jurisdiction of the registrar at Halifax.
There is really no such trouble at all.
If there is no trouble, why the Bill?

The appointment of a deputy registrar in the Admiralty Court in Nova Scotia or in any other province should not be left in the hands of the irresponsible person who happens to be registrar. The position is an important one, and as the registrar himself is responsible to the government of the country, so should be the deputy, but he is responsible only to the registrar. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no intention at all of making a change in the personnel of the office. The same man will be reappointed, but his jurisdiction will be wider.

Section agreed to.
On section 2

Appointment of deputy judge.
What is the effect of this section?

There is nothing new in it. The late government passed a similar section in 1920, and we are amending that law so as to leave the sole power with the Governor in Council. Under the law passed in 1920 the jurisdiction in the matter of the appointment of the deputy, was left either with the Governor in Council or with the local judge. We are abolishing the jurisdiction of the judge and leaving it entirely with the Governor in Council. That is the only difference between this legislation and the act of 1920.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT

speechtext: On motion of Hon. H. S. Beland (Minister of Health) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the Chair:

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
That it is expedient to amend The Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, chapter 17 of the statutes of 1911, as amended by chapter 31 of the statutes of 1920 and chapter 42 of the statutes of 1921, and to provide:-
1.	That subsection one of section five of the said act be amended so as to provide that a written order shall be required in connection with all sales of narcotics to druggists and others, and that it shall be unlawful to refiill narcotic prescriptions except where the preparation might lawfully have been sold in the first instance.
2. That subsection two of section five be amended so as to provide that it shall be unlawful for any physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist to prescribe, administer, give, sell or furnish any drug to any person except for medicinal purposes, or as may be prescribed for the medical treatment of a person who is under professional treatment.
3. That subsection two of section 5A be amended to prescribe heavier penalties for manufacturing, selling, giving away or distributing drugs without license, ana for neglect-;ng or refusing to keep the record required by the regulations.
4.	That section 7 be amended to empower any constable or other peace officer who has reasonable cause to suspect that any drug is kept or concealed upon any premises to search for the same, and bring it before a magistrate having jurisdiction in the matter.
5.	That no person shall, without lawful authority or without a permit signed by the Minister of Health or some person authorized by him in that behalf, import or have in his possession any opium pipe, opium lamp or other device or apparatus designed or generally used for the purpose of preparing opium for smoking, or smoking or inhaling opium.
6.	That penalties be prescribed for violation of the provisions of the proposed legislation.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: Section 5 of the resolution provides that no person shall import or have in his possession any opium pipe, opium lamp or other device used for the preparing of opium for smoking, without lawful authority or without a permit from the Minister of Health. What legal purpose can there be in the importation of such apparatus? What has the minister in mind in contemplating their importation?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: If these devices for the consumption of op him are found in the possession of any person that person shall be subject to a penalty.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: The minister has not my point. We all know what a terribly dangerous thing opium is in itself, and I was wondering if it is possible that any useful purpose could be found for these appliances.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: Not that I know of.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: Then why is the minister reserving the power provided for in this paragraph?

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext:
Section 6 provides:
That penalties be prescribed for violation of the provisions of the proposed legislation.
In view of the fact that of 835 convictions last year 634 were of Chinese, would it not be advisable to incorporate, as a penalty, that all orientals found trafficking in drugs shall be deported? This would help to some extent to solve the oriental question in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: Such a provision would naturally have to be incorporated in the Immigration Act. As to the other penalties, they are fully described in the bill which will be introduced, based on this resolution. When the bill is before the House my hon. friend will see the penalties in each case. I shall be glad to explain the provisions in regard to the penalties because they vary, as applying to persons who have received a license, and to others who have not. So far as a provision for deportation is concerned, the committee will realize that it could not very well apply to Canadians. Only to Chinese, who have not been naturalized, could it apply. Personally, I have no objection to such a provision being incorporated in the Immigration Act, because I do not think that the country is profiting in any degree whatever by the presence of foreigners who administer, sell, or distribute narcotic drugs, especially to the younger people.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext:
I happen to have some knowledge in regard to investigations carried on into the illegal sale of narcotic drugs, both in Vancouver and in Winnipeg, and I know that the investigators were in all cases people of the highest responsibility in their respective communities. I understand that an investigation was also held in Quebec, and even in Ottawa. There is a certain psychological aspect to any legislation that will be effective in deterring men from carrying on this illegal sale. One effective deterrent is deportation, and I would urge upon the minister the wisdom of inserting in the bill a provision empowering the authorities to deport men or women convicted of the illegal sale of drugs or of the commission of other serious offences under the act. I would also strongly urge upon him the necessity of giving discretionary power to magistrates to order the lash in those cases where it is proved that the accused deliberately and cold-bloodedly induced young people to become drug addicts. This is neither the time nor the occasion to go fully into the matter, but there is

Opium and Narcotic Drugs
an appalling traffic in drugs. The addict must be treated as a patient. The trafficker, generally an oriental, a cool, calculating person, does not take the drug himself because he knows its terrible effects on those who become its slaves, but he ingeniously inveigles innocent people into the habit. He has a well-planned system of business, covering importation, wholesaling and retailing, and hon. members would be amazed if they knew what was disclosed to a representative committee which investigated conditions in Vancouver. The lash would be the most effective deterrent you could possibly apply, because one thing these traffickers do fear is corporal punishment. And surely a man or woman, white, brown or yellow, who deliberately induces young girls to become addicts is guilty of a more serious crime against society than robbery with violence. Scores of associations throughout Canada have passed resolutions most emphatically favouring the infliction of the lash upon these nefarious traffickers, and I hope the minister will see that the bill contains the necessary provision to this end.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext:
I heartily endorse what
the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) has just stated. We find that this traffic is increasing very rapidly in British Columbia, and is becoming a serious menace there, being largely, though not exclusively, engaged in by orientals. We feel that the penalities cannot be made too severe against those who profit from this nefarious traffic. Apparently the penalties now in force are inadequate, for they have not resulted in stopping the traffic. I would suggest that there be a much more vigorous application of the law by our police forces, and that they be made to realize the seriousness of this traffic, so that increased vigilance on their part will produce better results. I agree with my hon. friend that while many men will take chances of a heavy fine or imprisonment, they are fearful of receiving the lash, and that the prospect of such punishment and subsequent deportation would make them think twice before breaking the law. In a word, the deterrent effect of such penalties would be very helpful in putting down this traffic.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext:
To a very large extent
I share the views that have been expressed as to the proper punishment of those engaged in illicit drug traffic. Heretofore the infliction of the lash has been confined mainly to the punishment of physical crimes. But we are only considering the
principle at present, and after the bill has been given its second reading and is in committee, we can go over it clause by clause, and whatever course is agreeable I am willing to carry out.

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext:
When this
bill was up about two years ago we had the same question raised which is covered, as I recollect, by the first paragraph, which renders it unlawful for any chemist to refill a narcotic prescription. At that time representations were made, particularly by hon. members from the prairies, that in the West where many people lived great distances from doctors they very often could not get to the doctors in time to have their prescriptions refilled just when it might he absolutely necessary, to say nothing of the expense involved. It was thought that some degree of latitude should be given to druggists and a certain number of refills allowed. I wonder if my hon. friend has considered the objections raised at that time, and which must still obtain. I would also ask him what narcotic drugs can be supplied except under prescription. I thought we had stopped them all. This clause has an exception covering narcotic prescriptions which might have been "lawfully sold in the first instance." What is meant by that?

maintopic: THE OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT
speechtext: The law permits of certain preparations being sold which contain narcotic drugs in very small quantities. I have not in mind at the present moment what the exact quantity is for each teaspoonful, but it is so small that it was considered advisable that such prescriptions should be permitted, largely on the suggestion, I think, of some of the western members. It is felt that some relief should be afforded in cases where necessary without a prescription, and the law has been framed so as to permit the refilling by druggists of prescriptions containing certain small proportions of narcotics. It is these preparations that the present law refers to when it provides that they could be lawfully refilled as if they were ordinary prescriptions. But I can give my hon. friend further details when the bill is in committee.

I do not think tie exception refers to prescriptions at all; it refers merely to preparations which druggists themselves put up without the intervention of a doctor.
Mr. BELAND. That is what I have in m ind-preparations.

On motion of Hon. D. D. McKenzie (Solicitor General) Bill No. 124 to amend the Escheats Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 1-Escheat extended to property of defunct corporations.

What has led to the necessity for legislation of this character? I presume that it can only be applicable to land and only in those provinces of Canada which have not, as yet, been entrusted with their natural resources. Am I right or wrong in that presumption?

Evidently this refers to personal property which becomes the subject of escheat in the right of the Crown and the right of the Dominion. The present bill does not materially change the character of the Escheats Act as passed by this parliament in 1910, except that the original act contains no provision as to the period within which actions must be brought for or on behalf of the Crown. The present bill simply fixes the time within which action must be brought. I may say to the committee frankly that I am not very familiar with the act, never having conducted any proceedings under it. This bill comes to me from the Department of Justice, and it appears that in the working out of the act they have found it necessary to have such a provision.

Under section 2 an action must be brought against the government within two years. Now I know of no such limitation in actions except in civil proceedings for some form of violence, as in cases of assault, slander, or like

Escheats Act Amdt.
actions that everybody wants to see disposed of. In the province of New Brunswick an action for the recovery of land may be brought within twenty years, and under certain circumstances within forty years, so that it takes forty years to establish proscription in that province. The period may be less in some of the rest of the provinces; I think it is less in the province of Ontario. That is between party and party-between one subject and another subject-but here we are asked to say that action must be taken in the short space of twenty-four months. People may be absent and not aware of their rights; but, unless they approach the Crown and ask leave to sue within that short period, they are forever debarred. There must be some extraordinary reason moving the Department of Justice to ask for such legislation. I do not wonder the Solicitor General cannot comprehend it, and it is a most unfortunate thing that the Department of Justice did not furnish him with some memorandum showing the difficulties which had arisen and the need for action in this way. The only thing I can conceive is that possibly it is in aid of the Soldiers' Settlement Board. But if so, let him give the facts, and if the reasons appeal to us, we may he justified putting it through. I cannot justify a vote to destroy the right of heirs on a two years' limitation.
The first section is aimed at corporations. I can conceive that in those provinces where the title of the land is in the Crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada, and only in such cases, there may be a way in common law called escheat. That, simply, means that, in the failure of any heirs appearing, the Crown steps in and takes the property. The Crown has the power, and generally exercises it, of granting that land to the parties who are morally, though perhaps not legally, entitled to possession. The Crown meets cases of illegitimacy in that way, and it is quite right and proper that that should be done, but, with regard to land in the other provinces, I do not see that it can have any possible effect. Yet the language is very broad. Now, the attempt is to extend this to corporations. A corporation in one sense cannot die; in another sense it can, but if a corporation ceases to function legally, the people who are interested in that corporation have always a right to get the property by some process. It does not go to the Crown. I cannot think of a case where the property of a corporation
went to the Crown at common law, unless the corporation had forfeited its title in some way by some misconduct, but I cannot conceive of a case where a corporation can so utterly die that no person will be entitled to claim the estate. Suppose it was a company of five men; you have to presume that they are all deceased and that none of them has left any heirs. That is a very large assumption. Some extraordinary case must have occurred to cause the Department of Justice to ask the Solicitor General to introduce a bill of this kind, and why does the department not furnish him with the information, so that we can know the reason for passing this legislation? Until I have some such mandate before me, I am sure the Solicitor General will excuse me if I say it is not such legislation as, at first blush, commends itself sufficiently to warrant my support.

I might say that this measure comes from the Department of Justice. This bill was presented to me with the intention that I should introduce it, and I did so. A request was made that I should call on the deputy minister and get some further history in regard to it. I have been so busy with other matters that I have not found time to do that. The bill is here now, and I have to deal with it. We are not bound hard and fast to any number of years, and if we can agree upon any number of years-say four years if that would be satisfactory to hon. members opposite-I am sure the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) and the department have no particular purpose in placing the time at two years. The idea is to take hold of these properties and prevent them from lying idle and going to waste, where there are no heirs to take possession. The department has decided, in the shortest possible time, to put an end to these conditions. That is why it fixed this comparatively short period of time within which parties would have a right to bring action. In many cases the property is going to waste, falling to pieces, and nothing is to be gained by delay. It is rather hard to he waiting for many years, without closing the matter and disposing of the property. If we leave it open for any great length of time for anybody to step in and, rightly or wrongly, make a claim to the property, of course it affects the sale and final disposition of the property. These are the reasons that moved the department to provide a means of closing up the matter as quickly as possible, or to give the property to those who are entitled to it, if an action
Escheats Act Amdt.

is brought and somebody is found to be entitled to it. The department wants to make as^ short a job of it as possible, and not let it run from year to year. If my hon. friend from St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) thinks we ought to extend the time, under the circumstance, the Department of Justice has no purpose in view, except to do what is absolutely right, but it is not desirable that matters of this kind should remain open too long.

I hope that nothing I have said would intimate in any way that I thought my hon. friend was trying to obtain any advantage, because I have no such thought in my mind, but his explanation, or want of explanation, if he will pardon me for saying so, convinces me I am right in the conjecture I formed but had not expressed. The moment he said the bill had come from the Department of Justice, I came to the conclusion that this was a very bureaucratic measure and not needed, and that some over zealous official was asking for legislation, without thinking seriously of the consequences. The explanation, or want of explanation, convinces me that I was perfectly right. I do not think the change from two to four years is going to help much. As a lawyer, the Solicitor General must appreciate that he will not, by a bill imposing a limitation of two years or four years or any other short space of time, prevent the making of claims by people who have no claim. It is not the people who have no rights he is cutting off; it is the people who have rights. Suppose a man comes from England, gets a farm out West in one of the provinces where the Crown owns the soil, and he has a regular title to that farm. He is not married, so far as any one knows, and has no family. He is working alone, and some years elapse. He dies. How does the Crown know that there are no legitimate relatives somewhere? How do the relatives know this man	has died, if he is a man
who has, perhaps, not kept up very much correspondence with his family? My hon. friend will hardly expect that he should write a letter telling of his premeditated demise, or that his spirit should write a letter telling that he has actually passed out of this sphere. How do they know whether he is dead or not. But we pass this bill, and if claimants do not appear within two years, their title is dead. What right has the Crown in respect of Canada to that property? Somebody else paid for it; somebody else worked on it; somebody else earned it; and even if his 	'
relatives are somewhat remote in degree, they and not the people of Canada are entitled to that property. If that man's property has been invaded by some trespasser who had acquired a footing upon it, and if the man was away and did not know that, he would have, under the law of the western provinces, I think, twelve years in which to vindicate his rights. If it was in my province of New Brunswick, he would have twenty years.
In Ontario, ten years.

If he died before that term was up and his children were under age, a further time would be allowed to enable them to reach their majority and to vindicate their title. Why should the Crown ask for such a right as this, not a right to deny the title of a man who has no title, but a right to deny and extinguish the title of people who have good title? That is what it is. I cannot understand the mind of the man who drafted this bill. He cannot have thought of the consequences; he probably was thinking only of squatters coming in on the property; and if they were going to assert title, he wanted them to do that properly. I am in entire sympathy with that; but the Crown did not need the help of any new legislation for that; under the common law, the Crown could have taken that property and held it against the world except the rightful owner. The Crown does not need this bill to-day to do that. What is the emergency? What is the reason? I would feel much more content if my hon. friend would kindly consent to get the names of individual cases and mention them in this Chamber. There will surely 'be in the representation of this House some hon. members from the West who will recognize the cases if they are mentioned. Such cases are rare. In my province, a province of something less than half a million population, I can recall three instances in the last fifty years, and the province of New Brunswick has a general escheat law, but no such legislation as this, where grants are made when it is found that people are morally, although not legally, entitled. There can be no great number of cases and no great hardship. Would it not be better to bring us all the information, so that we might know why some official in the department got so exercised as to think it necessary to draft a law that would cut away, upon a two years' proscription, the rights of people lawfully entitled to property?

Escheats Act Amdt.

There is hardly a legal case or a case of law in regard to property, either real or personal, hut would be placed by my hon. friend in the extreme position which he has described. It would appear, according to his contention, that by reason of this legislation, severe hardships are to be inflicted upon certain individuals. It is a well-established principle that the Crown can do no wrong. On the Crown bringing this action, there must be service on somebody; there must be service of some kind or information that must be exhibited in connection with this action. The Crown cannot go on without somebody representing the supposed heir or whoever is supposed to have a right to this property. He must be represented before the court. Are we to take it for granted that the party who is appointed to represent the alleged heirs; or if there are heirs, after the service of these papers or their advertisement in the newspapers, in the Canada Gazette and in whatever other way the practice of the court and the order of the judge may direct-

Will my hon. friend permit me to interrupt him for a moment? There is no need for our having a misunderstanding of the plain wording of the law:
Where His Majesty the King, in his right of Canada, is entitled to any land or other real or personal property by reason of the person last seised or entitled thereto having died intestate and without lawful heirs the Attorney General of Canada may cause possession thereof to be taken in the name of His Majesty, or if possession is withheld may exhibit an information in the Exchequer Court for the recovery thereof.
There is no need to advertise for heirs or anything else. You simply take possession.

Supposing the Crown takes possession; the Crown holds possession; but before the Crown can part with the property, or pass it over to anybody else, there must be a judgment of a competent court to enable the Crown to do so. It is a well-established principle of British law that no person's right can be affected without notice; there must be notice. My learned friend will find, in the very early cases of the Supreme Court of Canada, that the principle was established, that no man's right to property, or any other tangible right, can be affected without notice. Courts can go on giving titles and judgments as much as they like; but while that decision in the Supreme Court of Canada holds, notice must be given
before anybody's rights can be affected by those performances at all. Therefore, the greater part of what my hon. friend has pictured cannot happen at all. I wish simply to point out that this is property which nobody claims. It stands there for two years. The Crown has possibly taken possession ten days after the man has died; the Crown has possession; it holds possession for two years. No heir appears or there is no claimant to the property, and it is found desirable to sell it. Then the Crown, within those two years, will put itself in a position, by judgment of a competent court, to dispose of the property, and it is for the Exchequer Court to say what provision should be made. Supposing a man has made improvements worth $2,000 to a property; the Exchequer Court will say to the Crown: "You may sell this property provided that, before you dispose of it or alienate the title, you must get that $2,000 and put it into the bank and leave it there awaiting any claimant ". All those rights will be preserved by the judge. All that we say is that these steps must be taken. We have a court to deal with these matters, and we have every reason to believe that, if there is no real, proper defendant before the court, a judge will be even more careful about what becomes of the property than if there was a real live defendant and claimant represented by counsel before him. I have no desire to appear solicitous in regard to this matter; I am quite willing that the committee rise and report progress on this bill and ask leave to sit again. In the meantime, possibly I can find out the real facts that have moved the department or some important official of it to ask for this legislation.
I thank my hon. friend for taking this course. I think it will clear the air. If the minister will give the House the information which I have requested, I think the House will be better satisfied.

I am not disposed to
take much exception to the bill or the object which it is sought to obtain by it. I do take exception to the very limited term, two years, which the bill proposes to fix as against any claim that may be made against the Crown. In my view, there should be some finality in all these matters. I agree also that the law of escheat is not so common in this country, and the ordinary practitioner has not had a great deal of experience of it. It is in-
Escheats Act Amdt.

voked only at odd intervals; and I think I am right when I say that in respect of personal property this bill will be of exceedingly limited application. It could only possibly apply to personal property in unorganized districts or territories of Canada. I think the law was settled as far back as the year 1883 in a case which went to the Privy Council from the province of Ontario. By the judgment of the Privy Council in that case-I think, the Attorney General of Ori-tario against the Attorney-General of Canada-it was settled that escheated estates became the property of the province and not of the Dominion of Canada. The application of this bill will be limited to real estate in those provinces where the Dominion still owns land, and to personal property only in the unorganized districts of Canada. So that in regard to personal property the application of the bill will be extremely limited. Practically, the bill deals only with real estate, and I for one think that in the case of a man dying without a will and without heirs there should be some finality in the matter of his estate, some final method of disposal. If it goes eventually to the Dominion of Canada, the right of the Dominion should at the earliest convenient time become absolute and action should be barred. I do think that the period of two years proposed in the bill is entirely too restrictive. If the Solicitor-General will recommend a period of six years, which is the usual term of limitation in respect of ordinary actions in law, or even longer, in regard to land, I personally do not see any great objection to the bill passing the House. Perhaps, in the interval, as the bill is not to be proceeded with to-night, the Solicitor-General could think out the question of a more extended limitation, and if he will submit a bill providing a period of six or even ten years, speaking for myself alone, I do not see any objection to the bill. I think it is a bill that should be passed.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
The amendments provide that whenever a judge, by reason

of age or infirmity, becomes incapacitated for the due execution of his duties, he shall cease to receive his salary, but this shall be done only on report of the Minister of Justice to the Governor in Council after an inquiry has been held by one or two judges or more of the Supreme Court, or a judge of the Exchequer Court, or one or more judges of the highest court of the province concerned, after notice has been given to the judge in the matter. On Section 8-Conveyance of cattle without proper rest, etc.-Carriage of calves under three weeks old.

Why is it an offence to carry a calf under the age of three weeks by boat or rail? I understand the object, but let me point out that a calf one week old is perfectly old enough to be shipped ten or twenty miles by boat or rail, and it is being done every day of the week. Why make it a criminal offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the old law. The only amendment is to strike out the necessary consent by the owner to keep the animals in any car or vessel for more than thirty-six hours.

That amendment may or may not be desirable, but what I am asking is why it is illegal for a common carrier to transport a calf less than three weeks old, when it is not harmful and is being done every day of the week. What is the use of having laws which are unreasonable, and are not being observed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is any good ground to amend the law I shall be willing to consider it.

My recollection is that this clause was inserted owing to representations made by very worthy citizens who constitute the Humane Society. It was represented that it was an act of cruelty
to ship calves under three weeks old without their dam.

I have always observed,
Mr. Chairman, that people who know most about farming are those who live in cities. It is not a cruelty to a calf to ship it when it is three weeks old unless it is shipped a very long journey without nourishment. A distance of twenty or thirty miles can be covered by boat or rail within four or five hours, and it does not injure the calf to have it go without nourishment for that length of time. Many of these societies for the prevention of cruelty to animals are very admirable societies, kept up largely by ladies who cannot be expected to be familiar with the intricacies of agricultural life. In the state of nature, which is supposed to be the nearest we can get to proper conditions, a cow will leave its calf cached somewhere for nearly a whole day while it goes out for food, and will come back and nurse the calf at night, with no resulting injury to the calf. As a matter cf fact, I am told that this section was introduced with some vague idea of restricting the shipping of calves which are not pure-bred, but I do not know about that. I think this is an unreasonable provision.

With regard to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, some hon. members will recall that three sessions ago there emanated from the same society the suggestion that it would be unholy or criminal to use poison gas on grasshoppers because it might injure without killing them. It seems to me that the sentiment expressed in this present provision is similar to the sentiment which was expressed on that occasion. What the hon. member (Mr. Neill) says concerning the feeding of calves is quite right; I have known the dam to leave her young for twenty-four hours without causing the slightest injury. As a matter of fact, if you tried to catch the calf during that period you would find it a very strong youngster and quite capable of keeping out of the way. I think that this is an unwarranted intervention.

The section says that it shall be illegal to ship calves under three weeks of age other than calves at foot of milch cows, or purebred calves. In other words, if a calf is under three weeks old it must not be shipped unless it is purebred. What peculiar quality is there in a purebred animals which enables it to do without nourishment longer than one which is not purebred?

On section 11-certain fines in Ontario to be paid to the municipalities.

Why does this apply
only to Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Representations have been made by the province of Ontario on this point, and they seem to be unanimous. That is why the amendment is made in relation to Ontario.

The distinction is quite clear. In Quebec the provincial government provides for the building of the court houses and the like, as well as all the machinery for the administration of justice. In Ontario the municipalities build the court houses and maintain them. It seems right, therefore, that the municipality should get this very small recompense arising out of the administration of justice.

What my hon. friend has said with regard to Ontario applies equally to New Brunswick, and I think, to Nova Scotia as well. In both these provinces the municipalities build the court houses and meet all the cost of admin-

What is the reason for the increase?

It is the usual increase of business, and is based upon the estimate

of last year.. Last year there was not quite sufficient to cover the amount required, and we had to put through some orders in council and supplementaries.

Under this item, I
notice, there is an increase in last year's expenditure of $125,000. I do not wish to enter into that feature of this estimate, but wish to bring another matter before the committee in connection with the estimate. It is a matter that was mentioned in this House some two years ago, it has come before the Department of Trade and Commerce a number of times, and it was taken up with the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) when he was Prime Minister, I believe that he and the Department of Justice have had correspondence on the subject. I refer to the case of one of my constituents, Mr. J. A. Campbell, of Sovereign, Saskatchewan, who shipped a car of flax in November of 1916 to the Acme Grain Company, of Winnipeg, Manitoba, with instructions to sell the flax when it reached a certain price. On February 2nd, 1917, Mr. Campbell enlisted and went overseas. 'In April of 1917, while Mr. Campbell was overseas, the car of flax was sold, because flax had reached the stipulated price, but the Acme Grain Company defaulted. Their liabilities were $35,000, and their assets, which were represented by the guarantee bond they had obtained, were but $7,500. Mr. Campbell's flax was sold for $2,894.55, but, when he got his share of the bond, he received only $621.86, being a net loss to him of $2,272.69, and this loss was sustained over five years ago. Mr. Campbell claims this amount, with interest, for a period of something over five years. I might enter into some proof of the legal ground for his claim. I will read some sections of the Canada Grain Act, which are not very lengthy. Section 210 reads:
Any person desiring to carry on the business of grain commission merchant in the western inspection division shall make application in writing to the hoard for a license to sell grain on commission, stating the locality where he intends to carry on such business, and the probable amount of business he will do monthly.
Then section 211 reads:
On receiving such application the board shall fix the amount of a bond to be given to His Majesty with sufficient surety for the benefit of persons entrusting such commission merchants with consignments of grain to be sold on commission.
In section 213, provision is made for the issuing of a license to such company on

payment of a fee. The board referred to in this legislation is the Board of Grain Commissioners, which is under the supervision of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which department is a department of this Government, which Government represents the people of Canada. Mr. Campbell claims that this Department of Trade and Commerce should make good his claim. I am well aware that the Department of Justice has ruled that Mr. Campbell his no legal claim on the department, so that I do not care to enter into the controversy and try to prove that he has. If he has not a legal claim, I am quite sure that he has a moral claim. This is the case of a Canadian citizen. He is a resident of my constituency, and I know him personally. He went overseas, and for nearly two and one-half years was in the service of his country. For about seven months of that time he was in hospital. We can easily imagine the thoughts that a person would have while overseas presumably to protect our interests as well as his, on hearing that his property at home was looted to the extent of over $2,200. We can easily imagine what kind of effect it would have upon him to get word from the Department of Trade and Commerce that he had no legal claim to recover this loss. He might easily reason that Britain had no legal right to go into war to protect Belgium. Indeed, I question if she did have any legal right; but yet she went in because she had a moral right, and to show that she had that moral right, about 1,000,000 of her sons gave up their lives. Also he might reason that, even though Britain went into the war, Canada was not legally bound also to go in. Yet Canada went into the war and about 50,000 of her sons are mouldering in Flanders to-day, not because she was legally bound to go, but because she felt morally bound to go. Therefore, if the department is not legally bound to make good this claim, it seems to me that this gentleman, a returned soldier, has a moral claim on the finances of this country. I might refer the committee to item No. 168 on page 43 of the Estimates, where we passed in this committee an expenditure of $5,000 to provide for the building of a tablet to the memory of the late Bowman B. Law, who lost his life in the fire which destroyed the old Parliament building. When this item was going through, I was revolving in my mind what claim there was on the Government of 180
Canada to make this expenditure of $5,000.
I did not raise any question in opposition, because I, like the rest of the committee, felt that, perhaps, there was a moral responsibility on the Government to make this payment. If there is a moral responsibility on the country to pay out $5,000 in this case, there is a greater moral responsibility on the Government to pay out something over $2,200 to make good an actual loss for one who left his country and left his property in the care of the citizens of Canada.
There is another item in the Estimates, that for militia annual drill. We recall quite well in this committee that we made provision to expend $1,100,000 for the ensuing year on annual drill. While there was some opposition to this item of expenditure, it went through. During the discussion, the point was raised that it was very necessary to keep up annual drill in order to have people in shape in case of some future possible war. The expenditure of $1,100,000 under this item will not have as far-reaching effect as the payment of this just claim against the Department of Trade and Commerce. I make this statement because the injustice done to this individual is known throughout western Canada. He is the type of individual that does not let a small matter drop. He is the kind of individual that made good at the front because he is the kind that sticks to and hangs on when there is a point to be gained. He has written in several of our western papers; he has corresponded with the Department of Trade and Commerce. I venture to say that they have a voluminous correspondence over this case. He has also corresponded with the Department of Justice, with the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment, with the exPrime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and with the Great War Veterans' Association. His correspondence has reached tremendous proportions, and this has been going on for several years, so that the case is very well known in western Canada. He has taken the matter up with western members; there are other members in this House who are well acquainted with the facts in this case. Others suffered loss through the defaulting of this company; but Mr. Campbell, to the best of my knowledge, at least, is the only returned man who has suffered loss in this way. Therefore, I would suggest that his case be given favourable consideration. I am aware that I would not be within my rights to



Supply-Canada Grain Act
move that this estimate be increased to make provision for this loss; but I would submit to the minister of this department that, in bringing down his supplementary estimates, he make provision for taking care of this liability.

I desire to associate
myself with the hon. member for Kin-dersley (Mr. Carmichael) in support of the contention which he has just presented. I am personally acquainted with Mr. Campbell, and I am aware that he has no legal claim against the Government. I believe, however, he has a moral claim in this regard. The board, appointed by this government, were directed by the statute to provide a sufficient bond to protect him in the business which he entrusted to these commission grain merchants. They failed to provide a bond that was sufficient to cover his loss. He was at the front protecting the lives of the people of this country; he suffered a very severe loss, and he is a man who could ill afford to stand a loss of this character. He feels, and his associates, soldiers who were at the front with him and are now his neighbours, familiar with the circumstances, all feel, that while he has no legal claim he certainly has a moral claim upon this country, which he helped to defend. For that reason I sincerely hope that the suggestion of the member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) may receive the earnest consideration of the minister.

It is only fair to say that the member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael and the member for Battleford (Mr. McConica) have already urged Mr. Campbell's claim upon the Department of Justice. To-night they have put it upon a new ground, and I am glad to know that they have withdrawn the contention that Mr. Campbell has a legal claim. The matter has been fairly stated by the member for Kindersley. It has been several times reviewed by the previous government, and was referred to the Department of Justice. That department, having examined the Manitoba Grain Act and all the claims and pretensions of Mr. Campbell, have given their ruling that Mr. Campbell has no legal claim. Now, it is fair to say on behalf of the grain commissioners that the bonds upon grain companies are always based upon the previous year's business, and to add that while there were other firms willing to purchase grain, Mr. Campbell himself selected the Acme Grain Company, to whom he shipped his grain on the 
20th of November. On the 18th of December the bank surrendered the bill of lading to the Acme Grain Company. We have the statement that Mr. Campbell enlisted on the 19th of February, 1917, so it is apparent that Mr. Campbell was himself in the country when the bill of lading was surrendered to the Acme Grain Company. He cannot evade that share of responsibility. Mr. Campbell on the 7th of April, 1917, gave instructions to the Acme Grain Company to sell the grain afid in the month of May the company defaulted. Now, I am bound to say that my hon. friends have convinced me that upon compassionate grounds Mr. Campbell may have some claim upon the country. Even supposing that he himself had surrendered the bill of lading to the Acme Grain Company, whom he had selected among all others to ship his grain, it is fair to assume that had he been in the country before the company defaulted it is possible he would have crowded them and obtained payment. Therefore, having in mind that Mr. Campbell spent seven months in hospital, that he voluntarily enlisted and went to defend the country, I am prepared to admit that it is possible that a claim might be made out on compassionate grounds. But I am not prepared to-night to commit myself and say that the Government will recognize that claim. We will take into consideration the representations made by the members for Kindersley and Battleford and at a later date, if not this year, then during next session, make a statement as to what we shall do.

The case which has been brought before us this evening, peculiar and special though it be is by no means singular, for we know that whether grain companies are bankrupt after conducting their business in a proper way or not, these cases are coming before us continually. Last year I am informed that a grain company in the city of Edmonton defaulted to the extent of many thousands of dollars, and the people who had consigned their grain to it were the losers. Last winter, before I left for the session, we had a similar case in the city of Regina where another firm, the mem-

For the crop year 1920-21 the total value of the overages to be delivered to the government was $130,524.06. Accounts have been rendered for this amount, but no payments have yet been made.
To my mind that is a serious state of affairs, and I cannot refrain at this stage from asking hon. gentlemen who have opposed our demand for a new system of marketing grain: Can they wonder that the farmers of western Canada are up in arms against this condition of affairs and determined that it shall cease?' men?

The board will issue public terminal elevator licenses and private terminal elevator licenses.
The first fight was to get the warehouse receipts issued by these private elevators put on the same footing as those issued by the public elevators. The trade managed to secure that. A regulation was made governing the sample markets; it reads in this way:

Mixing, you will note.
-the handling and mixing of grain in such private terminal elevators.
That was the whole fight of the trade. When they talked about sample markets they wanted the right to mix the grain, and once they got that legislation through they cared nothing about the sample market. It is true the Government found a
